reason: Attacked hardest of the four, because it was the one verified at one remove, and it survived, and the locator I expected to break turned out to be right. Wording: I pulled the raw HTML of Roger Poole's LRB review of the Rosenmeier volume and read the sentence in its own words rather than through a summariser. Poole prints: Above all, he writes to his beloved Jette (in 1847), do not lose your desire to walk: every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it, and then runs on with an elision dash. That is the proposed line exactly, colon and semicolon included, quoted inside a review of the named translation, so it is Rosenmeier's English and not one of the loose renderings in circulation. The competing blog translation by Kaare Torgny Pettersen, Above all, do not lose the desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and away from every illness, is a different Englishing of the same Danish and is not what the card prints, which is the right outcome. The card stops at a full stop where Poole elides; the Danish at that point reads gaae fra den. Selv om man gik, a sentence break, so the full stop is the edition's and not invented. Recipient and number: an automated read of the LRB first told me Henriette Lund, the niece, and letter 262, and both were wrong. Letter 262 is the Henrik Lund bird letter further down the same review, and Poole never names his Jette at the walking passage. The University of Copenhagen's Kierkegaard research centre settles it: SK i et brev til sin svigerinde Henriette (Jette) Kierkegaard (1847), her gengivet efter B&A 150, s. 168, that is, a letter to his sister-in-law Henriette (Jette) Kierkegaard, 1847, Breve og Aktstykker number 150. Kierkegaard's Writings XXV follows the Danish numbering, so Letter 150, to Henriette Kierkegaard, 1847 is correct, and the popular attribution to the niece is the trap the card avoids. The content fits the recipient, who was bedridden. Source line 117 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote; tag Correspondence is the form; shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Kierkegaard at one of three from January, not banned; an 1847 letter in a 1978 translation, in scope. One thing remains unseen and the editor should know it: the printed Rosenmeier page was not opened, only quoted, and the secondary page reference pp. 214 to 215 is unconfirmed, which is why the source line rightly omits it. That is a residual, not a refutation.
